awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of an In-home Plant Hydroponics Device
awd_abstract_narration:
This I-Corps project is focused on the commercialization of a unique device that allows people to produce their own plant-based foods and potentially learn about healthy eating, while improving their diet. The technology uses algae to provide fertilizer for vegetable growth and allows for the simple and easy growing of micro-greens, greens, and herbs at home. The countertop device requires little space and no electricity to grow plant-based diet options for people in their homes and kitchens adjacent to where food is prepared. The advancement is designed to help people add affordable, healthy options to their daily routines and to learn about beneficial nutrition.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of a compact, in-home hydroponics device that uses algae to provide fertilizer for vegetable growth. The device uses tap water and has no complex wiring or electronics. The algae grow on the special interior of the device which is configured to create a moist and textured environment that supports the algal needs while still encouraging plant growth. Seedling germination and plant growth in the device takes place over the course of two to three days when growing microgreens and one week when growing other plants. Harvesting is possible within one week for microgreens and two to three weeks for other plants. The algae are hardy and self-regenerating, so they do not require replenishment even after multiple rounds of plant production.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Project Duration: April 1, 2025 – March 31, 2026

URBN Steamlab conducted extensive customer discovery following the NSF I‑Corps methodology, including structured hypothesis testing, iterative customer interviews, and capture of qualitative data using in vivo coding. USL tested the Value Propositon of a simple, compostable in-home growing unit for those interested in producing their own food through user testing, on-site piloting, and agriculture market research.

Across the I‑Corps regional and national programs, the team completed approximately 130 customer discovery interviews with stakeholders spanning:

  • Urban and suburban households (B2C);
  • Older adults and caregivers;
  • Residential elder care and disability service providers (B2B);
  • Health, food systems, and community‑based organization professionals.

Interviews focused on food procurement behaviors, challenges related to growing or accessing fresh produce, perceptions of indoor growing technologies, and interest in gardening as an educational or wellness‑oriented activity.

Total Customer Discovery Interviews: ~130

Primary Customer Segments Validated: TWO: business to consumer households; Business to Business non-profit residential care providers

Beachhead Market Identified: Residential elder care and disability service providers

Pilot Studies Conducted: 1 (Bancroft Garden Fresh Home Pilot, 8 weeks, Nov–Dec 2025)

Prototype Iterations Tested During Grant Period: 2+

Institutional Partners Engaged: Bancroft; community health and food system stakeholders

External Funding Proposals Submitted: 1 NSF Fast-Track SBIR

Key Commercial Outcomes: Refined value proposition; validated product-market fit; transition to SBIR phase

NSF I-Corps Interpretation: These metrics demonstrate successful completion of NSF I-Corps objectives by validating customer needs, reducing risk, and positioning the project for commercialization.

Participation in NSF I‑Corps fundamentally shaped the team’s approach to both technology development and market strategy. Key lessons include:

  • Early assumptions about consumer “desire to garden” were less predictive than needs around health, routine, and accessible activities;
  • Value propositions must be tailored differently for end users and institutional buyers;
  • Customer discovery must continue in parallel with pilots and R&D to reduce risk and guide iteration.
